topic: Why the US-Mexico border is stranger than you think
hook: Your hug through a metal fence is real, and that fence runs straight into the sea.
title: The US-Mexico Border Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
A fence you can hug through that runs into the Pacific, clocks that follow the border, a bridge from America to a Mexican airport, and a river that forced two countries to swap land. These are true facts about the US-Mexico border, from Friendship Park near San Diego and Tijuana to El Paso and Ciudad Juarez. Watch to the end for the strangest one.

#geography #borders #facts

scenes.narration: Your hug through a metal fence is real, and that fence runs straight into the sea.
scenes.headline: A Hug Through Steel

scenes.narration: At Friendship Park, families meet through thick mesh, while the US-Mexico border walks right into the Pacific Ocean.
scenes.headline: Border Meets The Ocean

scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you will see five more things about this border that sound fake but are true.
scenes.headline: Sounds Fake. Is True.

scenes.narration: One is a bridge that lets you walk from America straight into an airport in Mexico.
scenes.headline: A Bridge To A Plane

scenes.narration: Another is a river that moved, and forced two countries to argue over one patch of land for about a hundred years.
scenes.headline: A River Moved

scenes.narration: Stay for the last one. It changed the map in 1967, and you can still see the proof today.
scenes.headline: The Proof Is Still There

scenes.narration: First, the fence in the sea. Friendship Park sits where San Diego in America meets Tijuana in Mexico.
scenes.headline: Where Two Cities Meet

scenes.narration: It is inside Border Field State Park, right at the corner where the border meets the Pacific Ocean.
scenes.headline: The Last Corner

scenes.narration: The park was dedicated in 1971 by First Lady Pat Nixon, and the barrier back then was a simple wire fence.
scenes.headline: A Simple Wire Fence

scenes.narration: She said she hoped there would not need to be a fence at all one day. That did not happen.
scenes.headline: She Hoped For No Fence

scenes.narration: Over the years the barrier became stronger, and a fine metal mesh now covers the spot where families meet.
scenes.headline: A Fine Metal Mesh

scenes.narration: Families split by the border walk up to this mesh from both sides, and talk through the tiny holes.
scenes.headline: Families Meet Here

scenes.narration: People have pressed fingers through the holes, held hands, and on some days even shared a hug.
scenes.headline: Fingers Through Mesh

scenes.narration: On the Mexican side, the plaza is open to everyone. On the American side, visiting has long been limited.
scenes.headline: Two Sides, Two Rules

scenes.narration: Now look at the end of the fence. It does not stop at the beach. It walks right into the waves.
scenes.headline: The Fence Walks Into The Sea

scenes.narration: Metal poles stand in the surf, and the Pacific washes straight through the border without asking anyone.
scenes.headline: The Ocean Ignores It

scenes.narration: This whole border is more than three thousand kilometres long, running from this beach all the way to the Gulf of Mexico.
scenes.headline: Beach To Gulf

scenes.narration: It touches four American states and six Mexican states. And along the way, it gets stranger.
scenes.headline: 4 US States, 6 Mexican

scenes.narration: Next, two towns that share one name, and a wall running right between them.
scenes.headline: Two Towns, One Name

scenes.narration: Second, look at Nogales. There is a Nogales in Arizona, and a Nogales in Sonora, Mexico.
scenes.headline: Nogales And Nogales

scenes.narration: A tall fence runs down the middle, and the name means walnut trees in Spanish.
scenes.headline: Named After Walnut Trees

scenes.narration: Both towns grew up around the same railway crossing, so they started life as one place.
scenes.headline: Born As One Place

scenes.narration: Further west, Calexico in California and Mexicali in Mexico have names that mix both countries together.
scenes.headline: Calexico And Mexicali

scenes.narration: Calexico is California plus Mexico. Mexicali is Mexico plus California. Each name is a mirror of the other.
scenes.headline: Names As Mirrors

scenes.narration: Many families have relatives on both sides, and cross every day for work, school and shopping.
scenes.headline: Daily Crossings

scenes.narration: San Ysidro, near San Diego, is one of the busiest land crossings in the world.
scenes.headline: A Very Busy Gate

scenes.narration: Two cities, joined in their names, and divided by a steel wall you can see from either street.
scenes.headline: One Wall, Twin Cities

scenes.narration: That was the easy part. The next one is about time itself, and it breaks a rule you probably trust.
scenes.headline: Time Bends Next

scenes.narration: Third, a time rule that bends around the border.
scenes.headline: A Time Rule That Bends

scenes.narration: In October 2022, Mexico ended daylight saving time for most of the country. Those clocks stopped changing.
scenes.headline: Mexico Stopped Changing Clocks

scenes.narration: But the cities along the border were allowed to keep changing their clocks, to match the United States.
scenes.headline: Border Cities Kept It

scenes.narration: So Tijuana still moves its clocks with San Diego, while Mexico City, far away, stays put all year.
scenes.headline: Same Clock As San Diego

scenes.narration: That makes sense, because so many people cross every day. One shared clock keeps school and work simple.
scenes.headline: One Shared Clock

scenes.narration: We in India run one time for the whole country. Here, the border decides whose clock a town follows.
scenes.headline: India Has One Clock

scenes.narration: A border that changes your clock is odd. But the next one lets you walk to a plane in another country.
scenes.headline: Walk To A Foreign Plane

scenes.narration: Fourth, a walkway that crosses a border. It is called the Cross Border Xpress.
scenes.headline: Cross Border Xpress

scenes.narration: It is a covered bridge linking a terminal in San Diego with the international airport in Tijuana.
scenes.headline: A Covered Border Bridge

scenes.narration: It opened in December 2015, and it lets travellers cross the border without ever stepping out onto a street.
scenes.headline: Opened In 2015

scenes.narration: You buy a ticket, pass the border checks, walk across the bridge, and you arrive inside the Mexican airport.
scenes.headline: Ticket, Check, Walk

scenes.narration: Many travellers use it to fly from Tijuana, because the airport is only a short walk from the American side.
scenes.headline: Fly From Another Country

scenes.narration: So here, the border is not a fence. It is a hallway inside a building, with a plane waiting at the end.
scenes.headline: The Border Is A Hallway

scenes.narration: If you like strange places that sound fake but are true, subscribe, because we find a new one every day.
scenes.headline: New Strange Place Daily

scenes.narration: And now, a nation whose homeland the border cut in two, long before most of us were born.
scenes.headline: A Homeland Cut In Two

scenes.narration: Fifth, a people who lived here before the border existed. They are the Tohono O'odham Nation.
scenes.headline: Here Before The Border

scenes.narration: Their traditional homeland stretched across what is now southern Arizona and northern Sonora, in the Sonoran Desert.
scenes.headline: A Desert Homeland

scenes.narration: In the 1850s, the Gadsden Purchase moved the border through their land, and the homeland ended up in two countries.
scenes.headline: The Gadsden Purchase

scenes.narration: Today the Nation's reservation in Arizona touches the border for a long stretch, and members live on both sides.
scenes.headline: Members On Both Sides

scenes.narration: On much of that land there is no tall wall, only low vehicle barriers that stop cars but not walkers.
scenes.headline: Barriers For Cars

scenes.narration: Tribal leaders have long said a full wall would cut families, ceremonies and sacred places in two.
scenes.headline: Families And Ceremonies

scenes.narration: So here, the line was drawn straight through a living community, and it is still felt every single day.
scenes.headline: A Line Through A Community

scenes.narration: India has villages like this too, and you may have heard of some. But the next one is a children's game.
scenes.headline: Next: A Playground

scenes.narration: Sixth, a playground that crossed the border. Three bright pink seesaws did it.
scenes.headline: Pink Seesaws

scenes.narration: In July 2019, designers Ronald Rael and Virginia San Fratello fitted seesaws into the border wall near El Paso.
scenes.headline: Seesaws In The Wall

scenes.narration: The wall there has gaps between steel slats. They pushed the long pink planks right through those gaps.
scenes.headline: Planks Through The Gaps

scenes.narration: People on the American side and the Mexican side went up and down on the very same plank.
scenes.headline: Same Plank, Two Countries

scenes.narration: When someone pushed down on one side, someone in the other country went up. That was the whole point.
scenes.headline: Your Push, Their Lift

scenes.narration: It lasted only a short time, but the photos travelled the world, and you can still look them up.
scenes.headline: Photos Went Worldwide

scenes.narration: A playground made of steel slats and pink paint. And the last story is bigger than all of these.
scenes.headline: The Biggest One Is Next

scenes.narration: Seventh, a river that moved, and a border that had to move with it.
scenes.headline: A River That Moved

scenes.narration: First, the line itself. It was drawn after a war, and in 1848 a treaty gave America land that was once Mexico's.
scenes.headline: Drawn After A War

scenes.narration: Mexico lost roughly half of its territory then, and in Texas the line follows the middle of the Rio Grande.
scenes.headline: Half Of Mexico Lost

scenes.narration: But rivers wander. After a flood in 1864, the Rio Grande jumped south near El Paso and Ciudad Juarez.
scenes.headline: The Flood Of 1864

scenes.narration: Suddenly a patch of land called the Chamizal was on the American side, though Mexico said it belonged to them.
scenes.headline: Whose Land Is It?

scenes.narration: The two countries argued about that one patch for about a hundred years. Imagine a dispute lasting a full century.
scenes.headline: A Hundred-Year Argument

scenes.narration: In 1963 they signed a deal, and in 1967 America handed the land back to Mexico.
scenes.headline: America Handed It Back

scenes.narration: To stop the river wandering again, the Rio Grande there was forced into a straight concrete channel.
scenes.headline: A River In Concrete

scenes.narration: Today you can see that straight concrete river on a satellite map, with El Paso on one side and Juarez on the other.
scenes.headline: Visible On A Map

scenes.narration: A national memorial park now stands on the American side to mark the Chamizal settlement, so the proof is real.
scenes.headline: A Memorial Marks It

scenes.narration: So a hug through a fence, clocks that follow a border, a bridge to a plane, and a river that moved land.
scenes.headline: One Border, Many Surprises

scenes.narration: Remember the hug through the fence, where the border walks into the sea? That was only the start of how strange this line is.
scenes.headline: Back To The Fence

scenes.narration: Tomorrow: another place that sounds fake, but is real. Come back for it.
scenes.headline: Tomorrow: Another One
